about: The one record of how Common Shade's knowledge has changed, for /growing/ ('Watch Common Shade grow'), llms-full.txt and the exit card. One entry per change, reviewed by hand; tools/growth-candidates.js proposes candidates and never publishes. 'added' is the day the change reached the site (its merged pull request, 'pr'); 'event' is the date of the underlying work, as printed by its source or computed from its records ('span'). 'why' is Common Shade's reading; 'finding' is what a source says, quoted from text already on the site (the check confirms it appears there). 'links' join an entry to records on the map: basis 'record' when the connection is in the site's structured data, 'editorial' when it is our reviewed mapping. 'effort' names the check files behind the change; the page counts them into 'What it took to add this' and never types a number. Kinds, places, people and topics come from fixed lists (see tools/growth-text.js). IDs are stable.

entries.why: The framework moves cities from emergency response towards lasting change, with the people most exposed at the centre. It now informs the glossary, the planning checklist and the cities it names.

entries.why: Readers plan real protection from these pages. Saying what the evidence supports, and what it depends on, keeps a plan from resting on more than the evidence holds.

entries.title: How Singapore organises for heat, traced to its own sources

entries.title: A planning question for heatwaves longer than any on record

entries.title: Signals: which way heat policy is moving
entries.why: Announcements are the earliest sign of where heat policy is heading, but on their own they are weak evidence. Signals places each one on a ladder from announced to evaluated, starting with COP31 and this year's signals already on the site, so readers can weigh them rather than collect them.
entries.review: COP31 facts checked on GitHub against the UNFCCC's own pages; one claim set aside (Beat the Heat, whose pages blocked the check) and one not used (a presidency claim the page did not confirm); the year's signals reuse sources the site had already checked

links.why: Several signals are promises of money; the ladder shows which have been funded.
Most signals touch heat action plans: adopted, funded or delivered.

entries.title: COP31 opens: the climate behind this year's heat
entries.why: As COP31 opened, WMO reported that 2026 will be one of the four warmest years on record and that El Niño is set to bring more heat into 2027, while UNEP's Emissions Gap Report found that warming will overshoot 1.5 °C. Each was verified at its primary source before joining the COP31 watch on Signals.

event.what: WMO State of the Climate Update 2026

finding.text: The global average surface temperature for January to September 2026 was about 1.47 °C above the pre-industrial average
source: WMO, 2026: State of the climate in 2026 gives new meaning to phrase 'off the charts'

entries.review: First read in a press report; every claim verified on GitHub at WMO, PBL (UNEP's co-author) and AFP; items about floods and electrification left out as not about heat

effort.asked: What did the opening of COP31 say about heat, confirmed at the source?
effort.open: How heat appears in COP31's final decisions.

links.why: A strong El Niño into 2027 is a forecast that early action can use.

entries.title: A page for the AI agents that read the site
entries.why: More people now meet the site through an assistant than through a browser. /for-ai/ tells an assistant what Common Shade is, when it fits a person's question, how to cite it and what to avoid, and publishes the same record as JSON and plain text, so an assistant can represent the evidence as carefully as the site states it.
entries.review: Written only from standards the site already publishes; every count is calculated at build time; every endpoint it lists is checked to exist; it asks nothing of an assistant that conflicts with its user's wishes
action: Read the page for AI agents

links.why: The evidence labels and standards the page asks an assistant to pass on are explained there.
How to cite the site, and where the open data is, is set out there.

entries.title: Open files for the tools that read the web, and a privacy page
entries.why: Assistants and crawlers look for a site's files at standard addresses. Common Shade now publishes an agent directory, an OpenAPI description of its open data with examples, a change feed and a Markdown twin of every page, and says plainly on one page what it keeps and what it asks other services for.
entries.review: Each file lists only what exists, and a check fails naming the path if one is missing; the privacy page restates what the site's code does, with nothing added
action: Read what the site keeps and shares

links.why: The page for AI agents lists the new files.

entries.title: A Heat Tool Finder: which tool fits the decision in front of you
entries.why: People who plan, deliver or fund heat protection often know a decision but not the tool for it. The finder sets warning services, assessments, datasets, modelling tools and guidance side by side, with what each needs, what it gives and what it cannot tell you, and three illustrative workflows that combine them.
entries.review: A researched starter catalogue: each record says how far its source was reviewed, nothing is ranked or presented as tested, links were checked on GitHub, and a check holds the filters to the catalogue's own policy

links.why: Each tool profile ends with a next step in Common Shade's own workbench, such as Plan a response.
